How is the boundary layer structured beneath a tornado, the surface flow that feeds the vortex above it? Because field observations are challenging, much of what is known rests on theory. A classical asymptotic analysis predicts a composite layer: a thin viscous layer carrying the shear stress, capped by a thicker layer carrying the inward mass flux. We test this quantitatively using particle image velocimetry of a tornado-like vortex in a water tank. The measurements support the two-layer structure and expose a surprising feature within it: fluid is entrained downward at all radii, yet the inner layer still detrains mass into the outer layer.

Where do the heavy elements in our universe come from, and how accurately can we model their creation? Accurately predicting the abundances of elements produced in the weak rapid neutron-capture (r- process) requires rigorous quantification of nuclear reaction uncertainties far from stability. This work utilizes cross sections with uncertainty-quantified optical potential and considers both independent (uncorrelated) rate variations and rate variations fully correlated via the underlying optical potential. While fully correlated variations alter the covariance structure among elemental yields, they do not automatically reduce the overall uncertainty envelope. By identifying specific neutron capture rates that have the most leverage on the r-process element production, this work provides a roadmap for experimental and theoretical efforts to constrain key nuclear reaction rates.

Here, the authors propose a new concept of nonlinear pure spin current rooted in quantum geometry. A pure spin current carries electron spin sideways without a net charge current in the same direction, making it attractive for low-power devices. They predict a unique property that flipping the built-in electric polarization of a nonmagnetic material can reverse the pure spin current. This flipping behavior is absent in the conventional spin Hall effect, which has impeded potential applications of the spin Hall effect in spintronics for a long time. The systematic survey here identifies five crystal symmetry classes that allow this behavior, and quantum mechanical calculations predict it in five atomically thin ferroelectrics, paving the way for experimental detection and device application.
